title: What do you do for a living?
title_target: Кем вы работаете? — Kem vy rabotayete?
goal: Talk about your job and what you do, and master the first verb group — six endings for six persons, a pattern you'll use hundreds of times.
bekal: conjugate Group I verbs for all six persons
ask and answer what people are doing
use the verbs знать, понимать, читать, работать, делать

dialogs.title: Диалог — Small talk in the elevator
dialogs.intro: Ani meets a neighbor in the dorm elevator. Notice that Russian verbs change their ending for every person, even though the pronoun is still said.

lines.speaker: Сосед:
lines.id: Good morning! Are you a new student?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Yes, I study here. I'm learning Russian.
lines.literal: yes, I — here — study. I — learn — Russian — language.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Not everything. I understand when you speak slowly.
lines.literal: not — everything. I — understand, when — you — speak — slowly.

lines.speaker: Сосед:
lines.id: Good. I'll speak slowly. What do you do for a living?
lines.literal: good. I — will — speak — slowly. as-what — you — work?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Right now I don't work, I just study. And you?
lines.literal: now — I — not — work, only — study. and — you?

lines.speaker: Сосед:
lines.id: I work as a programmer. My wife works at a hospital — she's a doctor.
lines.literal: I — work — as-programmer. my — wife — works — in — hospital, she — doctor.

lines.speaker: Сосед:
lines.id: A little. Our English is bad, both of us.
lines.literal: a-little. we — both — badly — know — English.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: That's fine! My Russian is bad too. We're even.
lines.literal: nothing! I — badly — know — Russian. we — even.

lines.speaker: Сосед:
lines.id: Great. My name is Sergey. Welcome!
lines.literal: great. me — they-call — Sergey. good — coming!

notes: **Russian verbs have six endings, one for each person.** ⚠️ This is a real new load for English speakers: English only adds -s for he/she/it, and "work" otherwise never changes. In Russian работать becomes работаю, работаешь, работает, работаем, работаете, работают. The good news: there are only two sets of endings in the whole language — Group I in this unit, Group II in Unit 6.

**The pronoun is still said, unlike in Spanish or Italian.** Since the ending already shows who's doing it, technically *работаю* alone means "I work". But Russians almost always say *я работаю*. The pronoun is only dropped in very short or very casual sentences.

**Кем вы работаете? is literally "as what do you work?"** The answer uses the ending **-ом / -ой**: *работаю программист**ом***, *работаю врач**ом***, *работаю учительниц**ей***. That's the instrumental case, and at A1 you only need to recognize it in this one pattern. ⚠️ Don't say *Я работаю программист* — the ending is required.

**If you don't want to bother with the -ом ending, there's a shortcut Russians really use:** *Я программист* — "I'm a programmer". The verbless sentence from Unit 1. Completely natural, and it doesn't sound simplistic.
**Не always goes right before the verb.** *Я **не** работаю* — I don't work. No "do" to add, it never joins the word, never moves behind it, never changes form. One of the easiest things in Russian.

**Хорошо / плохо are used for language skills, as adverbs.** *Я плохо знаю русский* — my Russian is bad, literally "I badly know Russian". That's the standard pattern; don't look for a word for "skill".

**Доброе утро in the morning, добрый день during the day, добрый вечер in the evening.** All three are warmer than Здравствуйте and still polite. ⚠️ Notice the endings differ because of the noun's gender: утро is neuter (доброе), день masculine (добрый), вечер masculine (добрый).

grammars.title: Group I verbs — endings -ю / -ешь
body: The biggest group in Russian. Drop **-ть** from the dictionary form, then add the ending.
after: Other verbs that follow this pattern exactly: **читать** (to read), **делать** (to do, make), **думать** (to think), **слушать** (to listen), **гулять** (to go for a walk), **отдыхать** (to rest), **изучать** (to study a subject), **играть** (to play).

⚠️ Watch the sound, not just the letters: **-ет** is said *-yit*, **-ешь** is said *-yish*, because unstressed е reduces to *i*. Saying *ra-BO-ta-yet* instantly sounds like a foreigner spelling it out.

grammars.title: One key verb that breaks the pattern: жить
body: **жить** (to live) is used from the very first conversation, and its endings don't match its dictionary form. Learn it whole.
after: *Где вы живёте?* — Where do you live? One of the questions you'll hear and ask most often. The answer needs the prepositional case, which comes in Unit 10; for now this is enough: *Я живу в Москве.*

blocks.text: Most professions have their own female form, but not all, and usage varies. The third column shows which are safe to use.

blocks.title: Two ways to say your job
items: **Я врач.** — the verbless sentence, the easiest and most common way. Always correct.
**Я работаю врачом.** — with the verb and the ending **-ом / -ем / -ой**. Sounds a bit fuller; it often comes as the answer to *Кем вы работаете?*
⚠️ For professions with no female form (врач, инженер, юрист, менеджер), women use the same word: *Она врач*, not *врачка*. Only the verb changes, in past-tense sentences: *Она работа**ла** врачом*.
